passages.title: Structural Labour Migration and Domestic Demand
passages.text: In India, over the last decade or so, labour has been departing agriculture, but is only going to construction and unregistered manufacturing which are not markedly better jobs. Services, where labour tends to be most productive, are not generating the additional jobs the country needs. India will need 24 million or so jobs over the next decade. The new sector, e-commerce, can at best close only half the jobs gap. Only those sectors that drive domestic demand such as health and education can comfortably fill the other half.

passages.title: Substantive Rights and State Protection of Privacy in the Digital Age
passages.text: In India, the current focus on the right to privacy is based on some new realities of the digital age. A right is a substantive right only if it works in all situations, and for everyone. A right to free expression for an individual about her exploitation, for instance, is meaningless without actual availability of security that guarantees that private force cannot be used to thwart this right. The role of the State, therefore, is not just to abstain from preventing rightful free expression, but also to actively ensure that private parties are not able to block it.

passages.title: Ecosystem-Centric Water Management vs. Supply Augmentation
passages.text: One of the biggest ironies around water is that it comes from rivers and other wetlands. Yet it is seen as divorced from them. While water is used as a resource, public policy does not always grasp that it is a part of the natural ecosystem. Efforts at engineering water systems are thus efforts at augmenting water supply rather than strengthening the capacities of ecological systems.

passages.title: Asset Allocation, Risk Diversification, and Financial Portfolios
passages.text: Asset allocation is the most important investment decision we will ever make, and sadly, most of us do not give that decision the importance it deserves. We are adamant about seeking predictability with our future. We tend to think of investing in risky assets as extremely volatile and value eroding. We also dislike fluctuating returns and the loss of control of investment. We think our money is best left idle, unproductive but safe. There is no asset that is risk-free. We could lose our jobs, our homes can lose value, our banks can go bankrupt, our bonds can default, the government can collapse and companies we chose fondly may cease to exist. But we cannot live life assuming that all these extreme events are waiting to happen, and all at the same time. All these extreme forms of risks we know will not manifest at the same time.

passages.title: Regulation of Multi-Trait GM Crops and International Obligations
passages.text: Although most of the Genetically Modified (GM) crops cultivated now are genetically engineered for a single trait, in future, crops genetically engineered for more than one trait will be the norm. Thus, biotechnology's role in agriculture and the regulation of the same cannot be understood solely in the context of the current generation of GM crops. Instead, there is a need to take a comprehensive look, taking into account various aspects, including socio-economic impacts, so that the potential of the technology can be harnessed while minimizing negative impacts. Given the importance of biotechnology in developing varieties that can help in climate change mitigation and adaptation, not using biotechnology as a part of the climate change action plan cannot be an option. Domestic regulation of biotechnology cannot be viewed in isolation of trade policy and obligations under various international treaties and conventions.

passages.title: Volatile Foreign Private Capital and Domestic Technology Diffusion
passages.text: Private investment in general is volatile. Foreign private investment is more volatile because the available investment avenues are significantly greater (i.e., the entire world). Therefore, the responsibility of providing employment cannot be left to Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). The current FDI inflows are volatile over time and across sectors and regions, which is a necessary consequence of their search for the highest returns. The adverse consequences are unstable employment and an accentuation of income and regional inequalities. A probable positive consequence of foreign investment is the inflow of new technology and its subsequent diffusion. However, the technology diffusion is not at all certain because the existing state of physical and human capital in India may prove inadequate for the diffusion.

passages.title: Seasonal Monsoon Skewness and River Water Harnessing
passages.text: Many opportunities to harness the highly skewed, seasonal and spatial distribution of monsoon flows, which occur in a four-month period from June to September annually, have been lost. Since these few months account for most of the rainfall and consequent freshwater availability, the need for holding rainwater in reservoirs, for subsequently releasing it for use over the year, is a necessity nobody can afford to overlook. Climate change will continue to affect weather conditions and create water shortages and excesses. While millions suffer from droughts and floods, waters in the country's many rivers flow unutilized, and are discharged into the sea every year.

passages.title: Economic Freedom and Incentives for Human Capital Investment
passages.text: People will invest in education whenever they are granted the economic freedom to fully enjoy its benefits. Again, this is for the obvious reason that the return on education increases as the level of economic freedom rises. When people, thanks to lower tax rates, are allowed to retain most of the higher income that they gain from each incremental level of education, it makes eminent sense to invest in education. On the other hand, when the government decides to tax the higher income of educated individuals at even higher rates, it makes very little sense to invest in educating oneself further. The same incentives apply to parents who decide on whether to invest in their children's education.

passages.title: Financing Sustainable Urban Water Delivery and Sewerage
passages.text: Our urban bodies cannot possibly ensure sustainable delivery of water in our cities unless financing mechanisms are put in place. Water delivery requires heavy investment in collecting it from a natural source, treating it to make it potable, and laying a distribution network of pipes for delivery to the users. It also requires investments in sewerage infrastructure and sewage treatment plants so that the sewers can carry the wastewater to these plants to ensure that no untreated sewage is discharged back into natural water bodies. If our cities were rich enough to meet the entire cost, water could be delivered free. They are not.

passages.title: Agricultural Terms of Trade, Farm Investment, and Rapid Poverty Reduction
passages.text: In India, agriculture still engages about half of its workforce, and about 85 per cent of its farms are small and marginal. Compared to China and Vietnam, which have experienced fast structural and rural transformation, India's story is of slow transformation. As a result, poverty reduction in India was at a much slower pace during 1988-2014, compared to China and Vietnam. India's poverty reduction was slow during 1988-2005, but during 2005-2012, it accelerated dramatically — almost three times faster than during the earlier period. What did India do during this period? Research reveals that the relative price scenario changed significantly (by more than 50%) in favour of agriculture in the wake of rising global prices. This boosted private investments in agriculture by more than 50%. As a result, agri-GDP growth touched 4.1% during 2007-2012 as against 2.4% during 2002-2007. The net surplus of agri-trade touched $25 billion in 2013-2014; real farm wages rose by 7% per annum. All this led to unprecedented fall in poverty.

passages.title: The Irish Potato Famine and Monoculture Genetic Fragility
passages.text: Spanish ships in the late 16th century first brought the potato tuber from South America to Europe whereby in the early 19th century, it had become a reliable backup to cereal crops, particularly in the cold, rain-soaked soils of Ireland. The Irish were soon almost wholly dependent on the potato as their staple food. And they were planting primarily one prodigious variety, the 'Lumper' potato, whose genetic frailty would be cruelly exposed by the fungus 'Phytophthora infestans'. In 1845, spores of the deadly fungus began spreading across the country, destroying nearly all the Lumpers in its path. The resulting famine killed or displaced millions.

passages.title: Childhood Malnutrition and Lifelong Economic Loss
passages.text: India is at once among the fastest growing global economies and home to the largest number of malnourished children in the world. There are regions where malnutrition is not the exception but the norm. And across the country, malnutrition is the cause of death for roughly half the 1.3 million children who die before their fifth birthday each year. Even those children who survive suffer permanently from the damage that has already been done to their bodies and minds from not getting enough of the right foods and nutrients. Around 44 million children under 5 are stunted. That makes it harder for them to learn in school and subsequently earn a living as adults. Their lifetime earnings potential is almost a quarter less than that of their healthy peers.

passages.title: Pusa Arhar 16: Agronomic Potential and Crop Residue Management
passages.text: The pulse variety 'Pusa Arhar 16' has the potential to be grown in the paddy-growing regions of Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh and eventually in all of India. Its yield (about 2000 kg/hectare) will be significantly greater than those of the existing varieties and because its size will be uniform, it will be amenable to mechanical harvesting, an attractive feature for farmers in northern India who currently use this technology for paddy. Most important, Arhar straw, unlike paddy straw, is green and can be ploughed back into the soil. In paddy straw, the problem is the high silica content, which does not allow for easy decomposition. In the case of Arhar, the farmer, even after combine harvesting, just needs to run a rotovator to cut the leftover straw into pieces, which can be ploughed back and will decompose very fast. All this is difficult with leftover paddy stalks that cannot be easily salvaged or ploughed back. Farmers, therefore, choose the easiest option of simply burning it.

passages.title: Reservoir Rule Curves and Monsoon Flood Buffering
passages.text: In India, authorities always look to store the maximum amount of water in reservoirs during the monsoon season, which is then used for irrigation and generation of electricity during the summer months. It is an internationally accepted practice that the water level of a reservoir should be kept below a certain level before the onset of monsoon season. This is so that when monsoon rains come, there is space to store the excess rainwater and also so that water can be released in a regulated manner. But the authorities store the maximum amount of water in reservoirs even before the close of the monsoon, only to ensure greater electricity generation and irrigation.

passages.title: Limitations of 1991 Liberalization and Structural Economic Crises
passages.text: Economic liberalization in India was shaped largely by the economic problems of the government than by the economic priorities of the people or by the long-term development objectives. Thus, there were limitations in conception and design which have been subsequently validated by experience. Jobless growth, persistent poverty and rising inequality have mounted as problems since economic liberalization began. And all these years later, four quiet crises confront the economy; agriculture, infrastructure, industrialization and education as constraints on the country's future prospects. These problems must be resolved if economic growth has to be sustained and transformed into meaningful development.

passages.title: Resolution Mechanisms and Exit Frameworks for Indian Banks
passages.text: Bank credit to the industrial sector has started shrinking. Its decline has been a serious concern as credit growth is essential to revive investment. The problem's origins lie in the incomplete reforms of the last 25 years. An institutional change that should have followed the 1991 reforms should have been setting up of a resolution corporation for banks. In a market economy with booms and busts, banks should be allowed to be set up and to fail. Today, we cannot shut down banks because there is no proper system to shut them down. Weak loss-making banks continue to need more capital.

passages.title: Renewable Tech Learning Curves and the Push for Gas
passages.text: India has tremendous potential for solar energy. We all realize that we have to stop burning fossil fuels to meet our energy needs. But certain renewable resources are still going through their cost curves and learning curves to get the required amount of output. The Indian Government has strongly committed to its targets of reducing emissions by 33 per cent by 2030, and towards this it has initiated a strong push towards a gas-based economy and has also invested heavily in renewable energy. However, business houses are wary of investing too heavily in renewable energy at a time when the technology is not yet ready.

passages.title: Genome Editing: Molecular Scissors vs. Transgenic Modification
passages.text: Genome editing is different from genome modification. Genome editing typically involves finding the part of a plant genome that could be changed to render it less vulnerable to disease, or resistant to certain herbicides, or to increase yields. Researchers use 'molecular scissors' to dissect the genome and repair it, which is a process that occurs naturally when plants are under attack from diseases and can throw up new mutations that enable the plant to survive future attacks. This evolutionary process can effectively be speeded up now that it is possible to examine plant genomes in detail in laboratories, and create mechanisms through which the relevant genes can be altered very precisely.

passages.title: Solid Waste Management and Drainage System Synergies
passages.text: Many people understand the connection between solid waste management and health in terms of the consequences of unattended heaps of dry garbage which become home for flies and other vermin. However, there is another aspect that is not well-understood, that is, what happens when unscientific solid waste management combines with poor drainage and dumping of untreated sewage into drains which are meant to carry storm water during rains. The result is choked drains which are full of stagnant water breeding mosquitoes, resulting in the spread of water-borne diseases.

passages.title: Constitutional Rider on Religious Freedom and Equality
passages.text: In Part III of the Constitution, which assures people certain fundamental rights, Article 25 proclaims that "all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion". What people fail to notice is that this proclamation is prefixed with the words "subject to public order, morality, health and to the other provisions of this Part", which set conditions precedent for the legal protection of religious practices of any community. The closing words of this prefatory rider in Article 25 virtually constitute a subordination clause placing other fundamental rights mentioned in Part III over and above the right to religious freedom. Among those other fundamental rights is the right to equality before law and equal protection of laws — assured at the outset and elaborated in later articles to mean, inter alia, that the State shall not deny equal protection of laws to any person or group of persons on the basis of religion alone.

questions.question:
How many zeroes are there at the end of the following product?
1 × 5 × 10 × 15 × 20 × 25 × 30 × 35 × 40 × 45 × 50 × 55 × 60
questions.explanation:
The number of trailing zeroes is determined by min(power of 2, power of 5). Since 5 occurs in every single term, powers of 5 far exceed powers of 2. We only need to count the exponent of 2 in the product:
- 10 = 2¹ × 5 -> one 2
- 20 = 2² × 5 -> two 2s
- 30 = 2¹ × 15 -> one 2
- 40 = 2³ × 5 -> three 2s
- 50 = 2¹ × 25 -> one 2
- 60 = 2² × 15 -> two 2s
Total powers of 2 = 1 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 2 = 10.
Therefore, there are exactly 10 zeroes at the end of the product.

questions.question: Let XYZ be a three-digit number, where (X + Y + Z) is not a multiple of 3. Then (XYZ + YZX + ZXY) is not divisible by
questions.explanation:
In place values:
XYZ = 100X + 10Y + Z
YZX = 100Y + 10Z + X
ZXY = 100Z + 10X + Y
Sum = 111X + 111Y + 111Z = 111(X + Y + Z).
Factoring 111 gives 3 × 37:
Sum = 3 × 37 × (X + Y + Z).
Thus, the sum is always divisible by 3, by 37, and by (X + Y + Z). Since (X + Y + Z) is explicitly NOT a multiple of 3, the sum has only a single factor of 3 and therefore CANNOT be divisible by 9.

questions.question: How many five-digit prime numbers can be obtained by using all the digits 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 without repetition of digits?
questions.explanation:
Any five-digit number formed by using all the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 without repetition has the sum of its digits equal to:
1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15.
Since 15 is divisible by 3, by the divisibility rule of 3, every such number is divisible by 3 and strictly greater than 3. Thus, every such five-digit number is composite, and zero prime numbers can be obtained.

questions.question:
In the sum
⊗ + 1⊗ + 5⊗ + ⊗⊗ + ⊗1 = 1⊗⊗
for which digit does the symbol ⊗ stand?
questions.explanation:
Let x denote the single digit represented by ⊗.
In place values:
- ⊗ = x
- 1⊗ = 10 + x
- 5⊗ = 50 + x
- ⊗⊗ = 10x + x = 11x
- ⊗1 = 10x + 1
- 1⊗⊗ = 100 + 10x + x = 100 + 11x
Sum LHS = x + (10 + x) + (50 + x) + 11x + (10x + 1) = 61 + 24x.
RHS = 100 + 11x.
Equating LHS and RHS: 61 + 24x = 100 + 11x => 13x = 39 => x = 3.

questions.question: If you have two straight sticks of length 7.5 feet and 3.25 feet, what is the minimum length can you measure?
questions.explanation:
By Bézout's Identity, using two lengths a and b additively and subtractively, the minimum positive length that can be measured is their Greatest Common Divisor, gcd(a, b).
Convert to inches or quarter-feet:
7.5 feet = 750/100 = 30/4 feet = 30 × 0.25 feet.
3.25 feet = 325/100 = 13/4 feet = 13 × 0.25 feet.
gcd(7.5, 3.25) = gcd(30/4, 13/4) = gcd(30, 13) / 4 = 1 / 4 = 0.25 foot.

questions.question: A simple mathematical operation in each number of the sequence 14, 18, 20, 24, 30, 32, ... results in a sequence with respect to prime numbers. Which one of the following is the next number in the sequence?
questions.explanation:
Notice that subtracting 1 or adding something reveals prime numbers:
14 − 1 = 13 (prime)
18 − 1 = 17 (prime)
20 − 1 = 19 (prime)
24 − 1 = 23 (prime)
30 − 1 = 29 (prime)
32 − 1 = 31 (prime)
The primes are consecutive prime numbers: 13, 17, 19, 23, 29, 31.
The next prime number after 31 is 37.
Therefore, the next number in the sequence is 37 + 1 = 38.

questions.question: One page is torn from a booklet whose pages are numbered in the usual manner starting from the first page as 1. The sum of the numbers on the remaining pages is 195. The torn page contains which of the following numbers?
questions.explanation:
A single torn leaf/page has an odd number on the front and the next consecutive even number on the back: (2k - 1) and 2k. Their sum is (4k - 1).
Let total pages in the booklet be n. Sum of all n pages = n(n + 1) / 2.
Remaining sum = n(n + 1)/2 − (4k - 1) = 195 => n(n + 1)/2 > 195.
For n = 19: 19 × 20 / 2 = 190 < 195 (too small).
For n = 20: 20 × 21 / 2 = 210.
Sum of torn numbers = 210 − 195 = 15.
Consecutive page numbers on opposite sides of a leaf summing to 15 are 7 and 8 (since 7 + 8 = 15, with 7 odd and 8 even).

questions.question: Let A3BC and DE2F be four-digit numbers where each letter represents a different digit greater than 3. If the sum of the numbers is 15902, then what is the difference between the values of A and D?
questions.explanation:
A3BC + DE2F = 15902. Available digits are from {4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9} (distinct and > 3).
Looking at column sums from right to left:
- Units: C + F must end in 2. Since C, F > 3, C + F = 12 (carry 1).
- Tens: B + 2 + 1 (carry) = 10 => B + 3 = 10 => B = 7 (carry 1).
- Hundreds: 3 + E + 1 (carry) = 9 => E = 5 (no carry).
- Thousands: A + D = 15.
Available digits from {4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9} not yet used: B=7 and E=5 are used. Remaining digits are {4, 6, 8, 9}.
From {4, 6, 8, 9}, pairs summing to 12 for (C, F): 4 + 8 = 12 => {C, F} = {4, 8}.
Remaining digits for {A, D} are {6, 9}. Indeed 6 + 9 = 15!
Therefore, {A, D} = {6, 9} in some order.
Difference |A - D| = |9 - 6| = 3.

questions.question:
Two Statements S1 and S2 are given below followed by a Question:
S1: There are not more than two figures on any page of a 51-page book.
S2: There is at least one figure on every page.
Question: Are there more than 100 figures in that book?
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above Statements and the Question?

options.text: Both S1 and S2 are sufficient to answer the Question, but neither S1 alone nor S2 alone is sufficient to answer the Question.
S1 alone is sufficient to answer the Question.
S1 and S2 together are not sufficient to answer the Question.
S2 alone is sufficient to answer the Question.

questions.explanation:
From S1: Figures per page <= 2. Total figures <= 51 × 2 = 102. (Could be 50, 100, 101, or 102). Insufficient.
From S2: Figures per page >= 1. Total figures >= 51. (Could be 60 or 200). Insufficient.
Combining S1 and S2: Total figures range from 51 to 102. The total could be 90 (not more than 100) or 102 (more than 100). Thus, a definite 'Yes' or 'No' cannot be reached even using both statements together.

questions.question:
Consider the following data:
[Category | Average marks in English | Average marks in Hindi]
Girls: English = 9, Hindi = 8
Boys: English = 8, Hindi = 7
Overall average marks: English = 8.8, Hindi = x
What is the value of x in the above table?
questions.explanation:
Let G be the number of girls and B be the number of boys.
In English: (9G + 8B) / (G + B) = 8.8 => 9G + 8B = 8.8G + 8.8B => 0.2G = 0.8B => G / B = 4 / 1.
Now calculate the overall average in Hindi (x):
x = (8G + 7B) / (G + B) = [8(4) + 7(1)] / [4 + 1] = (32 + 7) / 5 = 39 / 5 = 7.8.

questions.question: A family of two generations consisting of six members P, Q, R, S, T and U has three males and three females. There are two married couples and two unmarried siblings. U is P's daughter and Q is R's mother-in-law. T is an unmarried male and S is a male. Which one of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: There are 3 males and 3 females across 2 generations. Two married couples + two unmarried siblings. T is an unmarried male, U is female (P's daughter) and unmarried sibling to T (generation 2). P and S are males; Q and R are females (with R married to S, and Q married to P). Since Q is R's mother-in-law, Q is generation 1 and R is generation 2 married to Q's son S. Thus, R is S's wife.

questions.explanation:
Count days from 12 January to 12 July:
In a leap year (February has 29 days):
- Remaining days in Jan: 31 − 12 = 19 days ≡ 5 (mod 7)
- Feb: 29 days ≡ 1
- Mar: 31 days ≡ 3
- Apr: 30 days ≡ 2
- May: 31 days ≡ 3
- Jun: 30 days ≡ 2
- Jul up to 12th: 12 days ≡ 5
Total odd days = 5 + 1 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 5 = 21 ≡ 0 (mod 7).
Since the number of odd days is exactly 0, 12th July falls on the exact same day of the week as 12th January, which is Sunday! Thus, '12th July is a Sunday if the year is a leap year' is correct.

options.text: S1 alone is sufficient to answer the Question.
S2 alone is sufficient to answer the Question.
S1 and S2 together are sufficient to answer the Question, but neither S1 alone nor S2 alone is sufficient to answer the Question.
S1 and S2 together are not sufficient to answer the Question.

questions.explanation:
We need to find the largest among {P, Q, R, S}.
From S1: R > P and R > Q. Neither P nor Q is the largest. But S could be greater than R. Insufficient alone.
From S2: S is not the largest. Insufficient alone.

questions.question: The recurring decimal representation 1.272727... is equivalent to
questions.explanation:
Let x = 1.272727...
100x = 127.272727...
Subtracting the two equations:
99x = 126 => x = 126 / 99.
Divide numerator and denominator by 9:
126 / 9 = 14
99 / 9 = 11
Thus, x = 14/11.

questions.question: What is the least four-digit number when divided by 3, 4, 5 and 6 leaves a remainder 2 in each case?
questions.explanation:
The number must be of the form: N = k × LCM(3, 4, 5, 6) + 2.
LCM(3, 4, 5, 6) = 60.
We need the least 4-digit number (N >= 1000):
Divide 1000 by 60: 1000 = 60 × 16 + 40.
For k = 16: 60 × 16 + 2 = 962 (3-digit).
For k = 17: 60 × 17 + 2 = 1020 + 2 = 1022 (least 4-digit number).

questions.question: In adult population of a city, 40% men and 30% women are married. What is the percentage of married adult population if no man marries more than one woman and no woman marries more than one man; and there are no widows and widowers?
questions.explanation:
Let total adult men = M and total adult women = W.
Number of married men = 0.40M.
Number of married women = 0.30W.
Since each married man is married to exactly one woman: 0.40M = 0.30W => 4M = 3W => M / W = 3 / 4.
Let M = 300 and W = 400. Total adult population = 300 + 400 = 700.
Married men = 40% of 300 = 120.
Married women = 30% of 400 = 120.
Total married adults = 120 + 120 = 240.
Percentage of married adult population = (240 / 700) × 100% = 240 / 7 = 34 2/7%.

questions.question: What is the remainder when 51 × 27 × 35 × 62 × 75 is divided by 100?
questions.explanation:
Let P = 51 × 27 × 35 × 62 × 75.
Notice the factors: 75 = 25 × 3, and 62 = 2 × 31.
Thus, 25 × 2 = 50 is a common factor of P and 100.
Divide both P and 100 by 50:
P / 50 = (51 × 27 × 35 × 31 × 3) / 1.
Now evaluate (P / 50) mod 2:
All factors {51, 27, 35, 31, 3} are odd integers! The product of odd integers is odd.
Therefore, (P / 50) ≡ 1 (mod 2).
Multiplying back by the cancelled factor 50:
P mod 100 = 1 × 50 = 50.

questions.question: A sum of ₹ 2,500 is distributed among X, Y and Z in the ratio ½ : ¾ : ⅚. What is the difference between the maximum share and the minimum share?
questions.explanation:
Ratio of shares X : Y : Z = 1/2 : 3/4 : 5/6.
Multiply by LCM(2, 4, 6) = 12 to convert to integers:
X : Y : Z = 6 : 9 : 10.
Sum of ratio terms = 6 + 9 + 10 = 25 parts.
Total sum = ₹2,500. Value of 1 part = 2500 / 25 = ₹100.
- Maximum share = Z = 10 parts = 10 × 100 = ₹1,000.
- Minimum share = X = 6 parts = 6 × 100 = ₹600.
Difference between maximum and minimum shares = 1000 − 600 = ₹400.

questions.question: For what value of n, the sum of digits in the number (10ⁿ + 1) is 2?

options.text: For any positive integer n only

questions.explanation:
Test whole numbers (non-negative integers):
- For n = 0: 10⁰ + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2 (sum of digits is 2).
- For n = 1: 10¹ + 1 = 11 (sum of digits is 1 + 1 = 2).
- For n = 2: 10² + 1 = 101 (sum of digits is 1 + 0 + 1 = 2).
- For any whole number n >= 0, 10ⁿ + 1 = 100...001, which always consists of two 1s and n−1 zeroes. The sum of digits is always 1 + 1 = 2. Thus, it holds for any whole number n.

questions.question: In a class, there are three groups A, B and C. If one student from group A and two students from group B are shifted to group C, then what happens to the average weight of the students of the class?

options.text: No conclusion can be drawn due to insufficient data.

questions.explanation: The average weight of the students of the ENTIRE CLASS is given by (Total weight of all students in the class) / (Total number of students in the class). Shifting students internally between groups A, B, and C does not add or remove any student from the class, nor does it alter the weight of any student. Thus, both the total weight and the total headcount of the class remain identical, so the overall class average remains the same.

questions.question: How many different sums can be formed with the denominations ₹50, ₹100, ₹200, ₹500 and ₹2,000 taking at least three denominations at a time?
questions.explanation:
There are 5 distinct denominations available: {50, 100, 200, 500, 2000}. Notice that every distinct subset of denominations produces a unique sum because no combination of smaller denominations equals a larger one or another combination.
We must take at least three denominations at a time (subsets of size 3, 4, or 5):
- Subsets of size 3: 5C3 = 10
- Subsets of size 4: 5C4 = 5
- Subsets of size 5: 5C5 = 1
Total distinct sums = 10 + 5 + 1 = 16.

questions.question: How many different 5-letter words (with or without meaning) can be constructed using all the letters of the word 'DELHI' so that each word has to start with D and end with I?
questions.explanation:
The word 'DELHI' has 5 distinct letters: {D, E, L, H, I}.
The word structure is: D _ _ _ I.
The first position is fixed with D (1 way), and the last position is fixed with I (1 way).
The remaining 3 middle positions must be filled using the remaining 3 distinct letters {E, L, H}.
Number of ways to arrange 3 letters = 3! = 3 × 2 × 1 = 6.

questions.question: A bottle contains 20 litres of liquid A. 4 litres of liquid A is taken out of it and replaced by same quantity of liquid B. Again 4 litres of the mixture is taken out and replaced by same quantity of liquid B. What is the ratio of quantity of liquid A to that of liquid B in the final mixture?
questions.explanation:
Initial volume V = 20 L of liquid A. Quantity removed and replaced x = 4 L. Number of operations n = 2.
Remaining volume of Liquid A after n operations = V × (1 − x/V)ⁿ:
Liquid A = 20 × (1 − 4/20)² = 20 × (1 − 1/5)² = 20 × (4/5)² = 20 × 16/25 = 64/5 = 12.8 litres.
Total volume remains 20 litres, so volume of Liquid B = 20 − 12.8 = 7.2 litres.
Ratio of Liquid A to Liquid B = 12.8 / 7.2 = 128 / 72 = 16 / 9 = 16:9.

questions.question: The average score of a batsman after his 50th innings was 46.4. After 60th innings, his average score increases by 2.6. What was his average score in the last ten innings?
questions.explanation:
Total runs after 50 innings = 50 × 46.4 = 2320 runs.
After 60 innings, new average = 46.4 + 2.6 = 49.0.
Total runs after 60 innings = 60 × 49.0 = 2940 runs.
Runs scored in the last 10 innings = 2940 − 2320 = 620 runs.
Average score in the last ten innings = 620 / 10 = 62.

questions.question: As a result of 25% hike in the price of rice per kg, a person is able to purchase 6 kg less rice for ₹ 1,200. What was the original price of rice per kg?
questions.explanation:
Let original price be P per kg. New price = 1.25P per kg.
Original quantity = 1200 / P. New quantity = 1200 / 1.25P = 960 / P.
Difference in quantity = 6 kg:
1200 / P − 960 / P = 6 => 240 / P = 6 => P = 240 / 6 = ₹40 per kg.

questions.question: A person X can complete 20% of work in 8 days and another person Y can complete 25% of the same work in 6 days. If they work together, in how many days will 40% of the work be completed?
questions.explanation:
X completes 20% (1/5) in 8 days => Full work by X takes 8 × 5 = 40 days. (Rate = 1/40 per day).
Y completes 25% (1/4) in 6 days => Full work by Y takes 6 × 4 = 24 days. (Rate = 1/24 per day).
Combined daily work rate = 1/40 + 1/24 = (3 + 5) / 120 = 8 / 120 = 1/15 of work per day.
They complete 100% in 15 days.
Time to complete 40% (2/5) of the work = (2/5) × 15 = 6 days.

questions.question: A car travels from a place X to place Y at an average speed of v km/hr, from Y to X at an average speed of 2v km/hr, again from X to Y at an average speed of 3v km/hr and again from Y to X at an average speed of 4v km/hr. Then the average speed of the car for the entire journey
questions.explanation:
Let distance between X and Y be d. Total distance for the 4 legs = 4d.
Total time = d/v + d/(2v) + d/(3v) + d/(4v) = (d/v) × (1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4) = (d/v) × (12 + 6 + 4 + 3) / 12 = (25/12) (d/v).
Average speed = Total distance / Total time = 4d / [(25/12)(d/v)] = (48 / 25) v = 1.92v.
Since 1.92v lies strictly between v and 2v, the average speed lies between v and 2v km/hr.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
statements: 1. The minimum number of points of intersection of a square and a circle is 2.
2. The maximum number of points of intersection of a square and a circle is 8.
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: If a circle is tangent to one side of a square from the inside or outside, they intersect at exactly 1 point! (Or if they are completely disjoint, they intersect at 0 points). Thus, the minimum number of points of intersection is not 2. Statement 2 is correct: A circle can intersect each of the 4 straight line segments (sides) of a square at at most 2 points, giving a maximum of 4 × 2 = 8 points of intersection. Thus, only Statement 2 is correct.

questions.question: A man takes half time in rowing a certain distance downstream than upstream. What is the ratio of the speed in still water to the speed of current?
questions.explanation:
Let speed in still water be u and speed of current be v.
Downstream speed = u + v. Upstream speed = u − v.
Time taken downstream is half the time taken upstream: T_down = (1/2) T_up.
Since distance d is constant, speed is inversely proportional to time:
u + v = 2(u − v) => u + v = 2u − 2v => u = 3v => u / v = 3 / 1 = 3:1.

questions.question: How many pairs of natural numbers are there such that the difference of whose squares is 63?
questions.explanation:
We need natural numbers a, b such that a² − b² = 63 => (a − b)(a + b) = 63, where a > b >= 1, so (a − b) and (a + b) are positive integer divisors of 63 with (a − b) < (a + b).
Factor pairs of 63 = d1 × d2 with d1 < d2:
1. 1 × 63: a − b = 1, a + b = 63 => 2a = 64 => a = 32, b = 31 (Check: 32² − 31² = 1024 − 961 = 63)
2. 3 × 21: a − b = 3, a + b = 21 => 2a = 24 => a = 12, b = 9 (Check: 12² − 9² = 144 − 81 = 63)
3. 7 × 9: a − b = 7, a + b = 9 => 2a = 16 => a = 8, b = 1 (Check: 8² − 1² = 64 − 1 = 63)
There are exactly 3 such pairs of natural numbers: (32, 31), (12, 9), and (8, 1).

questions.question: Which one of the following will have minimum change in its value if 5 is added to both numerator and the denominator of the fractions 2/3, 3/4, 4/5 and 5/6?
questions.explanation:
Let original fraction be a/b. Adding 5 gives (a + 5)/(b + 5). Change = (a + 5)/(b + 5) − a/b = [b(a + 5) − a(b + 5)] / [b(b + 5)] = 5(b − a) / [b(b + 5)].
Here each fraction has b − a = 1! So Change = 5 / [b(b + 5)].
To minimize this change, the denominator b(b + 5) must be maximized! Thus, the fraction with the largest denominator b will experience the minimum change.
Denominators: b = 3, 4, 5, 6. The largest denominator is b = 6 for 5/6.
Check values:
- 2/3: 7/8 − 2/3 = 5/24 ≈ 0.208
- 3/4: 8/9 − 3/4 = 5/36 ≈ 0.139
- 4/5: 9/10 − 4/5 = 5/50 = 0.100
- 5/6: 10/11 − 5/6 = 5/66 ≈ 0.076 (minimum change!).

questions.question: A digit n > 3 is divisible by 3 but not divisible by 6. Which one of the following is divisible by 4?
questions.explanation:
n is a single digit with n > 3, divisible by 3, but not divisible by 6.
Multiples of 3 between 4 and 9: {6, 9}.
Since n is not divisible by 6, n must be 9! (Check: n = 9 > 3, div by 3, not div by 6).
Test the options for n = 9:
- (a) 2n = 2 × 9 = 18 (not div by 4)
- (b) 3n = 3 × 9 = 27 (not div by 4)
- (c) 2n + 4 = 18 + 4 = 22 (not div by 4)
- (d) 3n + 1 = 3(9) + 1 = 27 + 1 = 28 (28 is divisible by 4: 28 / 4 = 7!).
Thus, 3n + 1 is divisible by 4.

questions.question: If 1 litre of water weighs 1 kg, then how many cubic millimetres of water will weigh 0.1 gm?
questions.explanation:
1 litre = 1000 cm³ = 1000 × (10 mm)³ = 10⁶ mm³.
1 litre of water weighs 1 kg = 1000 grams.
So, 1000 grams corresponds to 1,000,000 mm³.
1 gram corresponds to 1,000,000 / 1000 = 1000 mm³.
0.1 gram corresponds to 0.1 × 1000 = 100 mm³.

questions.question: A vessel full of water weighs 40 kg. If it is one-third filled, its weight becomes 20 kg. What is the weight of the empty vessel?
questions.explanation:
Let the weight of the empty vessel be V and the weight of full water capacity be W.
1) V + W = 40 kg
2) V + (1/3)W = 20 kg
Subtract equation (2) from equation (1):
(2/3)W = 20 => W = 20 × 3 / 2 = 30 kg.
Substitute W into equation (1):
V + 30 = 40 => V = 10 kg.
The weight of the empty vessel is 10 kg.

questions.question: A frog tries to come out of a dried well 4.5 m deep with slippery walls. Every time the frog jumps 30 cm, slides down 15 cm. What is the number of jumps required for the frog to come out of the well?
questions.explanation:
Total depth of well = 4.5 m = 450 cm.
On each jump, the frog leaps up 30 cm and slides down 15 cm, achieving a net gain of 30 − 15 = 15 cm per jump, EXCEPT on the final jump when it reaches or exceeds the top (450 cm) and climbs out without sliding back down!
Threshold to reach before the final jump = 450 − 30 = 420 cm.
Number of jumps to reach 420 cm = 420 / 15 = 28 jumps.
After 28 jumps, the frog is at 28 × 15 = 420 cm.
On the 29th jump: from 420 cm, it jumps up 30 cm, reaching 420 + 30 = 450 cm (the exact top of the well) and gets out!
Total jumps required = 29.
